claims.text: Protective oxide development and retention in high-temperature HEAs is governed by a uniform elemental distribution.
Uniform elemental distribution minimizes local depletion of oxide-forming elements such as Cr and Al.
The proposed elemental uniformity stems from high configurational entropy.
Elemental uniformity promotes formation of a continuous and adherent oxide scale.
The resulting scale resists spallation and excessive growth more effectively than scales on non-HEA systems of similar overall composition.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the homogeneous dispersion of key oxide-forming elements.
A homogeneous distribution enables a steady and continuous supply of oxide-forming elements to the surface.
The continuous supply of oxide-forming elements promotes rapid development of a dense, adherent protective oxide scale.
The protective oxide scale has self-healing characteristics.
Segregated microstructures develop local depletion of oxide-forming elements.
Local elemental depletion causes discontinuous oxide-scale formation and faster degradation during high-temperature oxidation.
Relative to the segregated baseline, the uniform HEA will form a thinner oxide layer.
Relative to the segregated baseline, the uniform HEA will form a more uniform and adherent oxide layer with less spallation.
Relative to the segregated baseline, the uniform HEA will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics.
The proposed mechanism applies under high-temperature oxidation conditions in which diffusion governs oxide-scale formation.
The proposed mechanism requires sufficient oxide-forming elements, such as Cr or Al, in both compared materials.
Very high or cyclic thermal stresses may cause aggressive oxide spallation regardless of microstructure.
The magnitude of oxidation-resistance improvement may vary with alloy composition, processing conditions, and test environment.
